blocks.text: Meanwhile I confess that I do not rely much on that last argument, taken from the ten cors which each of that people is believed to have gathered. For there was no need for each person to gather ten cors of quails. God had promised this people meat for a month, and he would have fulfilled this promise if, instead of ten cors, he had given each person only a third of a cor. This is easy to prove. To each of the Israelites an omer of manna is assigned as daily food, Exod. XVI, 16, that is, the tenth part of an ephah, in the same place, verse 36 [var. 35]. And an ephah is the tenth part of a cor, Ezech. XLV, [col. 106] 11. Therefore a cor contains a hundred omer measures. And if an omer suffices for a day, a cor suffices for a hundred days, that is, for three months and more. Accordingly, if each of the Israelites gathered ten cors of quails, they gathered more than thirty times what God had promised. But when Moses says that even he who had gathered least gathered ten cors, perhaps this is to be referred only to the heads of families; and wives, children and slaves are not counted in that census. Or, what I think truer, in that place עשרה חמרים are not ten cors but ten heaps. For חמר chomer also means heap. Thus in Habac. III, 15. חמר מים רבים is a heap of many waters. And in the same sense it is said of the frogs in Exod. VIII, 10. ויצברו אותם חמרים חמרים, And they gathered them into heaps, heaps, that is, into many heaps. And in Iudic. XV, 17. [var. 16.] חמרתים in the dual is two heaps. But also in this very passage עשרה חמרים, Onkelos renders עשרא דגורים, and the Arabic edited at Paris عشرة انابير [ʿashrat anābīr], and Erpenianus عشرة اجداس [ʿashrat ajdās], ten heaps. If you take it this way, Moses will not have defined precisely what measure of quails [II, 670] each person gathered, but will only have said that ten heaps were gathered by him who gathered least. Ten heaps, that is, very many, by a phrase familiar to the Hebrews, who everywhere use ten for many. Thus Gen. XXXI, 7: He has changed my wages ten times. Num. XIV, 22: They have tempted me now ten times. Nehem. IV, 6: They have told us now ten times. Iob. XIX, 3: These ten times you have reproached me, that is, many times. Levit. XXVI, 26: Ten women shall bake your bread, that is, many. 1 Sam. I, 8: Am I not better to you than ten sons? Eccles. VII, 19: Wisdom gives strength to the wise more than ten rulers who are in the same city. Zachar. VIII, 23: Ten men shall take hold of the skirt of a Jew, that is, very many. So, then, Moses will have said ten heaps of quails for many ^{(11)}. And that it should be translated thus rather than ten cors is suggested, besides what we have already said, also by this reason: that כור, cor, or חומר chomer, is a measure of grain, not of meat ^{(12)}. This observation is not worthless. For if each of the Israelites is said to have gathered ten cors of quails, their number will be enormous and will exceed all belief. Cornelius a Lapide, who tried to compute it in his Commentaries on this passage, reckons the figures so as to prove that the Israelites gathered about twelve thousand million quails. But we, instead of ten cors, maintain that each did not gather or consume even a third part of a cor. We do this not to diminish God's power, but so as not to do violence to faith by extorting from it more than God has revealed to us in his word ^{(13)}.

[II, 671] But, you will say, this at least is certain: Moses asserts that God fed all the Israelites with quails for a month, among whom there were six hundred thousand footmen. I admit too that this bird is less frequent in our regions than that such a thing could happen without a new creation. But in hot regions the matter is quite otherwise, for there the abundance of quails is far greater. Thus that in Greece nothing was more common than the quail may be gathered from these lines of the comic poet Aristophon on peacocks in Athenaeus, book 14.

Τὸν ταὼν μὲν ὡς ἅπαξ τις ζεῦγος ἤγαγεν μόνον, [Ton taōn men hōs hapax tis zeugos ēgagen monon,] Σπάνιον ὂν τὸ χρῆμα· πλείους δ’ εἰσὶ νῦν τῶν ὀρτύγων· [Spanion on to chrēma; pleious d’ eisi nyn tōn ortygōn;]

Of peacocks someone had once brought only a single pair, a rare thing in that age; but now there are more of them than quails. And that at Rome too they were cheap is shown by these lines of Juvenal against legacy-hunters, Satire 12.
He has three heirs; I should like to see who would spend a sick hen, closing its eyes, on so barren a friend: but this is too great an expense; no quail will ever fall for a father. — —
